articles.title: Syria removed: Which countries are still on the US ‘terror’ list – and why?
articles.summary: The US decision leaves three nations – Cuba, Iran and North Korea – on its ‘State Sponsors of Terrorism’ blacklist.
articles.body:
The United States has removed Syria from its list of State Sponsors of Terrorism (SSOT), marking another major shift in Washington’s relationship with the country following the fall of the Bashar al-Assad regime in December 2024 at the end of a brutal 14-year civil war.

“Today, Syria shakes off a dark stain and tears away a painful chapter of its past to embark on a path of development, reconstruction and rebuilding,” Syria’s President Ahmed al-Sharaa said in a speech on Tuesday.

US President Donald Trump had announced the planned removal in July, which had been in place since 1979. It took effect following a 45-day congressional review.

The US “terrorism” designation had triggered restrictions on foreign assistance, defence exports, certain financial transactions and the transfer of some dual-use goods – products which can have military uses, as well.

It can also cause banks and companies to be wary of doing business with a country because of the legal and compliance risks involved. The removal of Syria leaves Cuba, Iran and North Korea as the only countries currently on the US “terrorism blacklist”.

Syria had been on the SSOT list since 1979, when the government of Hafez al-Assad was accused by Washington of supporting armed groups opposed to Israel.

The designation continued when his son, Bashar al-Assad, assumed power in 2000 and lasted for the entirety of his rule, which came to an end when he was overthrown in a lightning strike on Damascus by rebel groups led by al-Sharaa in December 2024. Al-Assad and members of his family fled Syria and are currently under supervisory asylum in Moscow.

In July this year, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the decision to remove Syria from the list came following “formal assurances” from the Syrian president that the country will not “support acts of international terrorism in the future”.

Washington has also praised cooperation between al-Sharaa’s government and the US against the ISIL (ISIS) armed group, which had, at various points, seized control of swaths of Syrian territory between 2013 and 2019, during the civil war.

Al-Sharaa previously led the al-Nusra Front, an al-Qaeda affiliate, before breaking ties in 2016.

The “terrorism-sponsor” designation had remained a major obstacle for potential investors in Syria even after Washington dismantled its broader Syria sanctions programme in 2025.

Rubio has said lifting the designation will “unlock international trade and investment” and give Syria a chance to rebuild.

Sina Azodi, assistant professor of Middle East Politics at George Washington University, told Al Jazeera that being removed from the list brings “many benefits”.

“It will make access to the US-dominated international financial and banking system easier,” Azodi said. “All of these will help trade relations, investment and diplomatic relations more attractive.”

Which countries are still on the US ‘terrorism’ list, and why?

Iran has been designated a “state sponsor of terrorism” by the US since 1984, following the Iranian Islamic revolution and the deterioration of relations with Washington.

The US continues to accuse Tehran of supporting armed groups across the region, including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Yemen’s Houthi group and a variety of groups in Iraq and Syria. The designation has led to the sanctioning of Iran’s government, financial system, military and oil industry.

On Monday, the US announced sweeping new economic sanctions on Tehran and entities in other countries which the US says facilitate trade with it, in a bid to isolate the country from the global economy amid a diplomatic deadlock during the current US-Israeli war on Iran.

US relations with Cuba have remained fraught since the Cuban revolution in 1959, when Fidel Castro overthrew the US-friendly President Fulgencio Batista.

The country was first placed on the “sponsor of terrorism” list in 1982, with Washington accusing Havana of supporting armed revolutionary groups.

President Barack Obama removed Cuba from the list in 2015 during a brief diplomatic thaw. However, towards the end of his first term as US president, Trump restored the designation in January 2021.

The following Joe Biden administration announced in January 2025 that it intended to remove Cuba again, saying there was no information supporting the SSOT designation. However, Trump reversed that decision after returning to office.

Since January 29, the Trump administration has also imposed a crippling fuel blockade against Cuba and threatened trade tariffs against any country that exports fuel to the island nation.

North Korea was first placed on the US SSOT list in 1988, largely because of its role in the bombing of Korean Air Flight 858 in 1987, which killed all 115 people on board.

Washington removed North Korea from the list in 2008 as part of efforts to negotiate over its nuclear programme, but restored the designation in 2017 during Trump’s first term.

It has remained subject to extensive US sanctions largely because of its nuclear and missile programmes, weapons proliferation, and other security concerns.

In addition to its “state sponsor of terrorism” list, the US government has various sanctions programmes in place against countries, companies and individuals.

Russia is heavily sanctioned by the US for its war in Ukraine. The US has resisted placing Russia on the “terror list”, however, despite calls from some lawmakers since the Ukraine war began in 2022.

Earlier this month, the US Senate passed a package that imposes up to 100 percent tariffs on major nations importing Russian oil and gas. The measure, if passed by the House of Representatives, would affect countries like China and India, which are key importers of Russian petroleum products.

In the US’s own hemisphere, Venezuela has faced extensive US sanctions, including on its leaders and oil industry, most notably under Trump’s second term.

In December, in a new round of sanctions, Washington targeted four companies and their associated oil tankers, allegedly involved in transporting Venezuelan oil. Petroleum is Venezuela’s primary export.

Trump defended the sweeping sanctions as a means of combating the illegal drug trade, even though Venezuela exports almost none of the fentanyl that the administration has made a central focus of its crackdown.

In January 2026, former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores were abducted in a US military operation, after longstanding tensions between Washington and Caracas finally boiled over.

The Venezuelan presidency has since been filled by interim President Delcy Rodriguez, who has aligned the country more closely with US interests, which include control over the country’s oil industry. In April, the US lifted personal sanctions on Rodriguez, who Trump has described as “a terrific person”.

The US also eased sanctions imposed on Venezuela’s central bank and has issued temporary sanctions relief in the form of waivers authorising US companies and individuals to conduct business in some areas of Venezuela’s oil, mining and financial sectors. These waivers can be cancelled at any time, however.

What impact does the ‘terror’ listing have on countries?

According to Cuba-based filmmaker and independent journalist Ed Augustin, the designation “definitely makes regular people’s lives worse” in Cuba.

“What it does is it contaminates, so to speak, the word Cuba in the global financial system,” he told Al Jazeera. “It turns Cuba into a pariah.”

“It’s been very difficult for Cuba to purchase machinery and chemicals to produce pharmaceuticals because of over-compliance and because a lot of the companies, even when they’re not based in the US, refuse to sell to Cuba. So there’s an extraterritorial dimension to this.”

Last year, independent UN experts expressed dismay when Cuba was put back on the list, saying it “constitutes a regressive step not only for bilateral relations between these two countries, but most importantly for the human rights and well-being of the people in Cuba, with the most devastating impact on vulnerable groups, including women, children, older persons, and persons with disabilities”.

UN experts have also condemned the recent oil blockade on the country of approximately 11 million people, saying designating Cuba as an “unusual and extraordinary threat” to the US lacked credibility.

Syrian political analyst Ruslan Trad, a non-resident fellow at the Atlantic Council, said the Trump administration’s “embrace” of al-Sharaa personally, “underscores that SSOT status functions as much as a lever of bilateral relations and strategic signalling as a counterterrorism assessment”.

“That political logic cuts both ways for those still listed. So, as a practical upshot, the SSOT list functions less as an objective terrorism registry and more as a foreign-policy pressure valve,” Trad told Al Jazeera.

“For Cuba, Iran, and North Korea, the absence of that same relief means continued isolation from mainstream global finance, even where the original rationale for designation [state support for terrorism] is, in Cuba’s case especially, widely contested as outdated,” he said.

articles.title: Pumpkin spice invades summer as Americans kickstart fall traditions earlier than ever
articles.summary: Demand for pumpkin spice latte spiked two weeks earlier than 2021, and 49% of consumers now start Halloween shopping before October even begins.
articles.body: If it seems like fall décor and seasonal food and drinks are arriving earlier each year, it's not just in your head. Data show consumers are increasingly embracing "season creep" — shopping for seasonal products earlier than they did in years past. Younger consumers' enthusiasm for fall, a desire to plan ahead and retailers' efforts to extend seasonal spending may all be helping drive the shift. STARBUCKS TO PROMPT MORE TIPPING ON CARD PAYMENTS, FUELING 'TIP CREEP' BACKLASH Last year, the popular pumpkin spice latte (PSL) returned to Dunkin' on Aug. 20 and to Starbucks on Aug. 26. Both coffeehouse chains brought their fall offerings back a day earlier this year, with Dunkin' launching its fall menu on Aug. 19 and Starbucks bringing back its PSL on Aug. 25, Florida Today reported. Data from online grocery delivery and pickup service Instacart showed that in 2024, "the seasonal peak for orders containing pumpkin spice items occurred on September 17, a full 10 days earlier than in 2023." Demand also cooled sooner, according to Instacart, though orders for pumpkin spice items, such as flavored coffee creamers and yogurts, spiked again in November as Thanksgiving drew near. Food delivery service DoorDash reported in 2025 that "pumpkin spice is brewing sooner than ever." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER PSL demand spiked on Aug. 19, nearly two weeks earlier than in 2021, the company reported. DoorDash also found that grocery orders for ingredients used to make fall-inspired drinks at home began spiking in late July. According to the National Retail Federation (NRF), 49% of consumers said in 2025 that they would begin shopping for Halloween before October, compared with 34% a decade earlier. "More 18- to 24-year-old early shoppers say they look forward to fall or that Halloween is one of their favorite holidays, and they plan accordingly," the NRF reported. "Their early Halloween shopping isn't about 'impulse purchases,' but rather intentional planning ahead." Younger shoppers were much more likely to say they wanted to avoid the stress of last-minute shopping for décor and costumes, according to the NRF survey. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Seasons affect people's minds and behavior for several reasons, Michael Varnum, professor and social psychology area head at Arizona State University, told Fox News Digital. Some of these effects are physiological, such as the ways our bodies and hormones respond to changes in light, temperature and other climatic conditions throughout the year, he said. The way seasons cause changes in illness, travel or population may also cue changes in how we think and act, Varnum noted. "How we respond to seasons isn't purely driven by actual changes in the environment but is also shaped by other associations, traditions, rituals and schedules – spring break, back to school in fall, Halloween, Christmas, etc. – that are built into our society and what we learn from an early age," he said. Climate and the environment also likely play a part, he said, reasoning that hotter summers could make people more eager for the cooler weather of fall. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Varnum said it's interesting that our culture's comfort in and enjoyment of seasonal traditions are heavily shaped by a model of four seasons "that doesn't necessarily fit well with what actually changes in the weather and environment in all parts of the world." He also acknowledged that a big part of season creep may be driven by marketing. "My guess is that retailers and others hope to capture boosts in spending associated with holidays or seasonal shifts earlier with the idea that it might extend the period for which they'll see it in their sales," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He added that it would be "interesting to know whether such marketing might be more or perhaps less effective when there is more of a mismatch between the season being invoked and the actual weather or time of year."

articles.title: At least 95 killed in Nepal flash floods, hundreds of tourists missing
articles.summary: The death toll from severe flash floods in the mountainous region between Nepal and Tibet has risen to at least 98, with hundreds of people still missing on...
articles.body:
The death toll from severe flash floods in the mountainous region between Nepal and Tibet has risen to at least 98, with hundreds of people still missing on both sides of the border, according to Nepalese authorities and Chinese state media.

The office of the Nepalese prime minister said at least 95 people had died, with the bodies recovered yet to be identified.

Hundreds of people are unaccounted for in Nepal, including 391 foreign nationals, 93 Nepali nationals, 60 hydropower project workers and 44 Nepal Army personnel. The floods have destroyed 19 bridges and around 40 kilometres of paved roads, with authorities still assessing the extent of the damage.

China, meanwhile, reported three deaths and 265 people missing in Gyirong county in south-western Tibet, according to state media, citing an initial assessment by local authorities. The exact number of missing people was still being determined and rescue operations were continuing.

The devastating flash floods struck along the Bhotekoshi River in the mountains of central Nepal and the adjoining region of Tibet.

articles.title: EasyJet holiday: passengers describe ordeal after Tunisia to Belfast flight cancelled
articles.summary: On Wednesday, the airline was able to organise flights to return the stranded passengers to Belfast.
articles.body:
A passenger has described her experience as "hell" after she was one of dozens of people left stranded in Tunisia.

Lorraine Molloy's flight home was cancelled four days ago, with EasyJet initially telling her and the other passengers it had no other flights available for another 10 days.

In the early hours of Wednesday morning, the airline was able to organise flights to return the stranded passengers to Belfast.

EasyJet said the "welfare of our customers is our highest priority and we are very sorry for any difficulty this may have caused".

Molloy described her experience as "awful" and said the ordeal has cost her and her husband thousands of pounds.

BBC News NI understands more than 100 people were booked onto the cancelled flight that was due to leave Enfidha-Hamamet Airport for Belfast International.

In a statement, EasyJet said they "did all we could" to support customers, including providing hotel accommodation, meals and alternative flight options.

They added that they covered onward transfers home for those who required them after Wednesday morning's flight.

Molloy, who had been on holiday in Tunisia with her husband, said they received "no communication" from EasyJet.

"I haven't had one email from them," she said, adding that EasyJet told passengers "nothing".

"The staff just kept walking by. We asked questions, we got no answers.

"I was left to source everything myself, apart from the help of the group."

Molloy said that passengers had formed a WhatsApp group to share advice, and that she "would have been lost" without it.

She said that passengers were told by the captain that the plane had technical difficulties, which further exacerbated her stress.

"I wanted to come home but at the same time I didn't want to be put on a plane that I was unsure if it was safe or not."

Molloy added that the hotel room provided by EasyJet felt like "a dungeon".

"When I went into that room, I just cried my eyes out."

EasyJet said that "no issues with the hotel accommodation provided have been flagged to our team but if they are, we will always look into this feedback with our hotel provider".

Molloy said she is "happy and relieved to be home", but is still concerned about reimbursement.

EasyJet said they will "reimburse customers for expenses they may have incurred as a result of the cancellation".

Natalija Dovbijenko, who had been travelling with her husband and child, told BBC News NI the hotel provided by EasyJet was not clean, with bathrooms that did not work.

She said that even once the return flight had been arranged the experience remained stressful for her and her family.

"When we arrived in the airport, the staff from EasyJet couldn't find us, they said we weren't registered for the flight," she said.

"A lot of people started panicking, somebody started crying, screaming, because people were stressed."

EasyJet said that "all customers who wanted to travel on yesterday's flight were booked on".

"We contacted customers proactively with information on how to book onto the flight for free, and any customers who arrived at the airport without booking were provided with seats," they added.

"We also published a dedicated number for customers who needed to call us for further assistance."

Dovbijenko added that there was a lack of clarity from the airline throughout the experience, and that it felt like staff did "not know anything" about their flight.

She said there was also a lack of communication.

"We were just sitting in the airport, beside the gate, without any information.

"You have to communicate with the people. You have to treat us as people, not as animals. They literally just treat us as animals. Nothing was organised.

"Please talk to us, just give us some information."

articles.title: Fundraiser for police officers killed in A66 crash in Middlesbrough tops £1m
articles.summary: Cleveland Police Federation says it will split the money between the two officers' families.
articles.body:
A fundraiser for two police officers who were killed in a wrong-way crash has reached more than £1m.

PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough died during the early hours of Saturday when a Volkswagen Passat, going the wrong way on the A66 at South Bank, near Middlesbrough, hit their vehicle. The five young men in the Volkswagen also died.

Among the donations to the police officers' fundraiser, which was launched by the Cleveland Police Federation, was £4,000 from the Cleveland branch of the National Association of Retired Police Officers.

Its chair Grant Thorburn said the officers' deaths had "hit home hard" and that seeing the tributes and donations paid to them had been "humbling".

He said: "Once you're a police officer, you're always a police officer, so even after you retire, particularly in Cleveland, it's such a small, compact force, everyone knows everyone else."

The Police Federation's acting deputy national chair Paul Williams said there was "tremendous grief" among Cleveland officers.

"The policing family is deeply scarred by this incident," he said. "This just brings it home as to how vulnerable we actually are."

He said police officers were human beings who were your ordinary relatives, friends, parents, partners and colleagues.

The fundraiser will be split equally between the families of the two men to be used as they wish, according to the Cleveland Police Federation.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) previously said that officers had been pursuing the Volkswagen Passat seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when the Passat turned on to the dual carriageway.

PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough had been in a vehicle looking for the Passat after its cloned registration plates triggered an automated number plate recognition camera, although they were not involved in the pursuit, the IOPC said.

PC Blades, a 37-year-old father of two, was described by his family as a "beloved husband" and the "most devoted father".

"He may have left this world committed to the duty he believed in, but his greatest legacy will always be the love he gave to his family," his wife said, adding he would be "forever our super hero".

PC Clough had served in the Army, with one man saying he was a "true friend, fantastic soldier and I have no doubt even better police officer".

His family said he had a "fantastic sense of humour" and would jump "into action whenever needed".

They added he had been their "hero", always "willing to help anyone for any reason".

Tributes have also been made to the five young men who died in the Volkswagen Passat, but a community group has urged people not to graffiti buildings with messages.

Active Tees Valley made the appeal on Facebook after messages were spray-painted on the East Middlesbrough Events Centre - formerly the Middlebeck Social Club.

Messages on its walls included: "RIP The Boys", "Never Be Forgotten RIP The Lads", and the initials of those in the car with "Rest easy boys".

The Facebook post said: "We understand that people want to express their emotions and pay their respects, but damaging buildings that are being used to support local residents ultimately impacts the same community we are all trying to look after."

Police said 17 people, aged between 18 and 61, had been arrested across Teesside as part of an ongoing investigation into the lead-up to the crash.

They have been held on a range of offences, including possession of a firearm and being part of an organised crime group.

articles.title: Putin and al-Sharaa discuss Russia-Syria relations, deal on military bases
articles.summary: Syria has been in talks on the fate of Khmeimim and Tartous bases, which Russia used to support ousted Assad regime.
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa have held discussions, including on the fate of Russia's military bases in the Middle Eastern country.

During a telephone call on Wednesday, Putin affirmed Moscow's support for Syria's territorial integrity and reiterated Russia's rejection of Israeli attacks and violations of Syrian sovereignty, reports Syrian news agency SANA.

The Kremlin stressed that the discussion also concerned deepening political dialogue and cooperation in trade, among other areas.

The talks were aimed at further development of bilateral relations and strengthened cooperation, SANA noted.

However, the status of the Khmeimim airbase and Tartous naval base, which are highly strategic for Russia, remains the key topic between Damascus and Moscow.

The Kremlin said that Russia-Syria relations will continue through continued contact "at various levels" and that "both sides underscored the importance of the Memorandum of Understanding On the Reorganisation of the Khmeimim Air Base and the Tartus Material-Technical Support Point, signed on August 9".

Syria announced earlier this month that a deal had been agreed after 18 months of negotiations that will see Khmeimim and Tartous turned into "joint training and capacity-building centres", with Syria to take control of civilian facilities at both bases.

Russia backed former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad throughout Syria's 13-year civil war, intervening militarily to keep him in power and expanding the Russian footprint at the Khmeimim air base and Tartous naval base on the Mediterranean coast.

Since al-Sharaa led the ouster of the a;-Assad regime, Putin has worked to build relations with the new Syrian government and to secure the future of the bases, which are key to Russian efforts to maintain influence across the Middle East and Northern Africa.

articles.summary: Syria has been in talks on the fate of Khmeimim and Tartous bases, which Russia used to support ousted Assad regime.
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa have held discussions, including on the fate of Russia’s military bases in the Middle Eastern country.

During a telephone call on Wednesday, Putin affirmed Moscow’s support for Syria’s territorial integrity and reiterated Russia’s rejection of Israeli attacks and violations of Syrian sovereignty, reports Syrian news agency SANA.

The Kremlin stressed that the discussion also concerned deepening political dialogue and cooperation in trade, among other areas.

The talks were aimed at further development of bilateral relations and strengthened cooperation, SANA noted.

However, the status of the Khmeimim airbase and Tartous naval base, which are highly strategic for Russia, remains the key topic between Damascus and Moscow.

The Kremlin said that Russia-Syria relations will continue through continued contact “at various levels” and that “both sides underscored the importance of the Memorandum of Understanding On the Reorganisation of the Khmeimim Air Base and the Tartus Material-Technical Support Point, signed on August 9”.

Syria announced earlier this month that a deal had been agreed after 18 months of negotiations that will see Khmeimim and Tartous turned into “joint training and capacity-building centres”, with Syria to take control of civilian facilities at both bases.

Russia backed former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad throughout Syria’s 13-year civil war, intervening militarily to keep him in power and expanding the Russian footprint at the Khmeimim air base and Tartous naval base on the Mediterranean coast.

Since al-Sharaa led the ouster of the a;-Assad regime, Putin has worked to build relations with the new Syrian government and to secure the future of the bases, which are key to Russian efforts to maintain influence across the Middle East and Northern Africa.

articles.title: 11 visitors trapped as dangerous flash flooding tears through iconic national park
articles.summary: Eleven hikers became stranded at Bryce Canyon National Park during flash flooding Monday, with two people showing signs of hypothermia after their rescue.
articles.body: Eleven visitors became stranded during flash flooding at Bryce Canyon National Park in Utah after heavy rain swept through the area. The hikers, all adults traveling in four separate groups, became trapped around 2:30 p.m. Monday as floodwaters affected several popular trails, according to FOX 13 in Salt Lake City. While none of the hikers was swept away, conditions left the groups unable to continue safely, the outlet reported. MAN PLUNGES 120 FEET INTO CREEK WHILE TAKING PHOTO AT FAMOUS NATIONAL PARK About 15 to 20 members of the county's search and rescue team, emergency medical services and the National Park Service responded to help the stranded visitors. The rescuers had to wait for conditions to improve in order to move people out safely. The rescuers then helped the groups make their way out of the affected areas, according to FOX 13. Following medical evaluations, two hikers showed signs of hypothermia and were taken to a hospital. The other nine were released, the outlet reported. The flooding affected several of Bryce Canyon's well-known trails, including Fairyland Loop, Navajo Loop, Queen's Garden and Peek-a-Boo Loop, according to reports. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The incident came during the Southwest's monsoon season, a period Bryce Canyon officials had warned visitors about earlier this month. In a recent news release, the National Park Service said August and September can bring rapidly changing weather to the region, with seemingly clear conditions giving way to intense afternoon thunderstorms. Those storms can create hazards including flash floods, trail washouts, debris-filled waterfalls and rockfalls, according to the park service. "Weather in the park can shift quickly," the National Park Service warned in the news release, urging visitors to remain aware of conditions both where they are and upstream. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES Park officials also cautioned that flash floods can pose a serious threat inside the canyon and advised visitors to check weather forecasts and flash-flood potential before heading onto trails. "We want to help visitors enjoy their experience and take home memories that last a lifetime," Bryce Canyon National Park Superintendent Allana Olbrich said in the news release. "We also want to help them do so safely, and having good information and awareness of the conditions they may encounter in these natural environments can make all the difference in creating those lasting memories," Olbrich added. articles.title: 2015 Kathmandu earthquake, 2026 flash floods: Why Nepal is so susceptible to natural disasters
articles.summary: South Asia News: Nepal is once again confronting the destructive force of nature, with flash floods sweeping through communities along the Bhote Koshi and other rivers.
articles.body: Nepal is once again confronting the destructive force of nature, with flash floods sweeping through communities along the Bhote Koshi and other rivers, killing dozens and leaving hundreds missing. The disaster has devastated settlements, roads, bridges and hydropower infrastructure in northern Nepal, while a mudslide in Tibet has also caused deaths and left hundreds missing. Rescue operations have been complicated by swollen rivers, damaged roads and difficult mountain terrain.The scale of the disaster has also exposed Nepal's vulnerability to hazards that can quickly cross geographical boundaries. Officials have warned people to stay away from the banks of the Bhotekoshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers, while helicopters have been deployed to rescue people stranded by floodwaters. The same region experienced a deadly flash flood last year, when a glacial lake outburst in neighbouring Tibet killed at least nine people and damaged the bridge linking Nepal and China.The latest disaster has renewed questions about why Nepal is so susceptible to natural calamities. The answer lies in a combination of its location between two tectonic plates, steep and fragile Himalayan terrain, intense monsoon rainfall, rapidly changing glaciers and high exposure of communities and infrastructure to hazardous areas. A country caught between tectonic platesNepal sits along the boundary where the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates collide. The Indian plate is being pushed beneath and against the Eurasian plate at roughly 5cm a year, building enormous geological pressure that is periodically released through earthquakes.The devastating Kathmandu Valley earthquake illustrated the consequences of that vulnerability. The region's mountainous terrain can amplify the impact of earthquakes by triggering landslides, avalanches and road blockages, while dense settlements and vulnerable buildings can turn seismic activity into a humanitarian disaster.The Kathmandu Valley also has a deep layer of clay beneath it. During a strong earthquake, seismic vibrations can cause water-saturated soil to lose its strength and behave like quicksand, a process known as soil liquefaction. This can severely damage buildings, roads and other infrastructure.Earthquakes therefore do not remain isolated events in Nepal. A major tremor can set off a chain of secondary disasters, including landslides, avalanches, blocked rivers and damage to hydropower and transport infrastructure. Where mountains turn hazards into disastersNepal's geography makes the country particularly exposed to floods and landslides. Steep slopes and narrow valleys mean that water and debris can travel rapidly downhill, leaving little time for communities to respond.The latest Bhote Koshi disaster is an example of this cascading risk. Initial assessments suggested that an earthquake may have triggered an ice-and-rock avalanche or landslide, blocking the river before releasing a sudden surge downstream. Experts have described such events as "cascading hazards", where an incident high in the mountains rapidly becomes a flood disaster in settlements below.The risks are not confined to the mountains. Nepal's southern Terai plains are highly exposed to river flooding, inundation and riverbank erosion, while communities in the hills face landslides, debris flows and flash floods. Roads, bridges, schools, hospitals, irrigation systems and hydropower projects are frequently located in areas exposed to these hazards. A warming Himalaya is adding another layer of riskClimate change is making an already hazardous environment more unpredictable. Nepal is home to thousands of glaciers, and rising temperatures are accelerating glacier loss and changing snowmelt and river-flow patterns.Research cited in the material shows that ice loss across the Hindu Kush Himalaya has doubled since 2000. As glaciers retreat, lakes can expand behind unstable natural barriers, increasing the risk of glacial lake outburst floods, or GLOFs. These can send enormous quantities of water and debris into downstream valleys with little warning.Last year's deadly flooding in the same region was traced to the drainage of a supraglacial lake in Tibet. The current disaster may have had a different immediate trigger, but the repeated flooding demonstrates how vulnerable the region has become to changes in the high mountains.Climate change is also associated with more erratic rainfall and more intense extreme weather. Heavy monsoon rain can saturate already fragile slopes, triggering landslides and worsening river flooding. In a country where agriculture, hydropower, tourism and rural livelihoods depend heavily on climate-sensitive resources, the consequences can spread well beyond the immediate disaster zone. Why vulnerability is about more than natureNepal's exposure becomes more dangerous when natural hazards overlap with poverty, weak infrastructure and limited access to essential services. More than 80% of the population is exposed to some form of natural-hazard risk, according to the material provided.The most vulnerable include mountain communities, farmers, people living along rivers and unstable slopes, informal urban settlements, children, older people and households with limited financial resources. Damage to roads and bridges can isolate entire communities, while disasters can disrupt healthcare, education, water supplies and food production.Nepal has a National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority responsible for coordinating disaster preparedness, search and rescue, information systems and risk-reduction measures. But reducing losses requires more than emergency response after a disaster strikes.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Tim Curry, star of ‘Rocky Horror Picture Show’ and ‘It,’ dies at 80
articles.summary: Actor Tim Curry, best known for his memorable role as Dr.
articles.body: Actor Tim Curry, best known for his memorable role as Dr. Frank-N-Furter in the cult classic film “Rocky Horror Picture Show,” is dead, according to his longtime manager and friend Marcia Hurwitz. In a statement to NBC News, Curry’s representatives said he died peacefully at his home in Toluca Lake, Los Angeles on Tuesday. The Los Angeles Police Department said a death investigation report was completed late Tuesday night for an 80-year-old man at a home in Los Angeles, though police did not identify the body as Curry. His cause of death has not yet been publicly revealed. He was 80 years old. While the English actor cemented himself as a fan favorite for his portrayal of Dr. Frank-N-Furter in 1975’s “Rocky Horror Picture Show,” fans of campy horror and mystery films also remember him for his roles as Wadsworth in the movie adaptation of the beloved board game “Clue,” and as the evil clown Pennywise in the 1990 TV movie version of Stephen King’s book “It.” Curry had long been dealing with health issues following a massive stroke in 2012 that left him partially paralyzed and unable to walk. Born on April 19, 1946, Curry amassed hundreds of credits across film, television and theater throughout his career spanning more than five decades. Curry first began his acting career on stage as an actor in the London company of the musical “Hair,” before eventually heading to Los Angeles to focus on his movie and television career. Younger generations of fans also recognize Curry for playing Rooster Hannigan in the 1982 movie musical “Annie,” acting alongside comedy legend Carol Burnett and Broadway darling Bernadette Peters. Curry also brought to life Mr. Hector, the iconic Plaza Hotel concierge in the 1992 sequel to “Home Alone,” as well as the pirate Long John Silver in 1996’s “Muppet Treasure Island.” In 1991, Curry won a Daytime Emmy for voicing Captain Hook on the Fox animated series “Peter Pan and the Pirates.” He earned three Tony nominations throughout his career. His first nomination came in 1980 for originating the title role in Peter Shaffer’s “Amadeus.” His last Tony nomination came in 2005 for originating the role of King Arthur in “Spamalot.” In 1993, Curry got a Tony nomination for playing Alan Swann in “My Favorite Year.” Curry published his memoir “Vagabond” last year, in part, to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the “Rocky Horror Picture Show.” In it, Curry tells readers that while there were parts of him in each of his characters, he was none of them. “The distinctions between who I really am and who I’ve pretended to be as an actor have proven to be a source of great disappointment to some audiences. It has not caused me much personal distress beyond the periodic necessity to deter stalkers,” he wrote. In one of his last on-camera interviews, Curry is seen in a wheelchair speaking to “CBS Sunday Morning” in October 2025, telling Turner Classic Movies host Ben Mankiewicz he loved how acting gave him “the freedom of being somebody else.” Curry is survived by his nieces, Kate Lewis, Julia and Patrick Bullman and great nieces, Josephine and Georgina and nephew, Mark Lewis.

articles.title: 'Like a bomb exploded': How a 2000 feet wide glacier triggered deadly Nepal floods
articles.summary: South Asia News: The deadly flash floods that tore through Nepal’s Himalayan border region on Wednesday may have been triggered by a massive chunk of glacier breaking .
articles.body: The deadly flash floods that tore through Nepal’s Himalayan border region on Wednesday may have been triggered by a massive chunk of glacier breaking away high in the mountains and crashing into a river valley below. An initial analysis by geologists and glaciologists cited by The New York Times suggests the event was an ice avalanche — a sudden collapse in which a huge mass of ice falls from a glacier, generating a powerful surge of water, ice and debris.Satellite imagery indicates that a section of glacier about 2,000 feet wide snapped off almost cleanly and fell from an altitude of around 17,000 feet, according to Daniel Shugar, a geologist at the University of Calgary who studied the images. The block dropped nearly 4,000 feet before reaching the valley floor, sending pulverised ice and water towards the Lhende Khola river and, ultimately, the Bhotekoshi River near the Nepal-China border.“It looks like a glacier in the area basically snapped off in a clean break, allowing it to fall just over a vertical kilometre to the valley bottom,” Shugar told the NYT. Describing the aftermath, he said: “The bottom looks like a bomb exploded — it’s just deposits from the broken-up glacier.”How a huge mass of ice became a deadly floodThe scale and height of the collapse gave the falling ice enormous potential energy. Simon Cook, a glaciologist at the University of Dundee who also analysed the satellite imagery, said the impact could have pulverised the ice into a fast-moving mixture of water and debris.“This is a big chunk of ice that is stored at high elevation in the mountain, with a huge amount of potential energy,” Cook said, according to the NYT. “That ice just gets pulverized into water.”The flow then moved northwest through the valley towards the Lhende Khola and Bhotekoshi rivers, producing the sudden surge that swept through settlements, roads, bridges and hydropower infrastructure. Officials have warned that another flood remains possible because a blockage is still lodged upstream on the Lhende Khola.The exact sequence of events is not yet certain. A magnitude 4.4 earthquake was recorded in the region early Wednesday, while climate and disaster experts have also pointed to the possibility of an ice-rock avalanche. Scientists caution that it is too early to establish whether an earthquake played a role or to determine a single cause of the disaster. A warning from a rapidly warming HimalayaThe disaster struck an area that has suffered a similar event within the past 14 months. Climate experts at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development said the Lhende Khola had flooded twice during that period, with last year’s flash flood linked to an overflowing glacial lake in Tibet.Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist, said the latest flooding was triggered by an ice-rock avalanche from a glacier on the Nepal side that blocked the river before releasing a sudden surge downstream. He stressed the importance of early-warning systems in “a warming Himalaya”.The wider region is increasingly vulnerable to floods, landslides and glacier-related hazards as temperatures rise. Research cited in the reports indicates that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya are losing ice at an accelerating rate, with the pace of ice loss having increased sharply since 2000.The immediate disaster has left dozens dead and hundreds missing across Nepal and Tibet, while foreign tourists, workers and pilgrims were among those unaccounted for. Rescue teams have been deployed, but damaged roads, heavy sediment and unstable conditions have made access difficult.For the communities living along Nepal’s steep Himalayan valleys, Wednesday’s catastrophe offered a stark reminder of how quickly a seemingly remote change high in the mountains can turn into a deadly wall of water and debris downstream.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Portrait of Ann Widdecombe put up in Parliament for MPs' return
articles.summary: The framed photograph forms part of work by MPs to install a permament memorial for the former minister.
articles.body:
A portrait of Ann Widdecombe has been erected in Parliament to remember the former MP, who was found dead with serious head injuries last month.

The picture of the ex-Conservative minister was put up on Tuesday in Portcullis House, where many MPs' offices are located, in time for the return from summer recess next week.

It forms part of ongoing talks about a fitting memorial for the minister turned Reform UK spokeswoman, who died aged 78 after being found in her Devon home . Joshua Kerry, 28, has been charged with murder.

Helen Grant, Widdecombe's successor as MP for the area of Maidstone in Kent, said the portrait was "the start of a lasting tribute to Ann".

"I am delighted that the Speaker of the House of Commons has confirmed that this portrait of Ann Widdecombe will be on show in Parliament, following her tragic death earlier this year," Grant said.

Work is underway "to explore a more permanent commemoration on the Parliamentary estate", she added.

The chosen photograph was taken in 2010 in the Cloister Corridor of the Palace of Westminster.

It is understood the portrait will remain in the coming weeks, while discussions continue among MPs and parliamentary authorities about a permanent fixture.

Widdecombe served as MP for Maidstone and The Weald for more than two decades until 2010.

Grant campaigned before MPs left Westminster for the summer recess for a memorial plaque to be installed in Parliament for Widdecombe, as was the case for former MPs Jo Cox and Sir David Amess, after they were killed while in office.

A shield commemorating Sir David was installed in 2023 a couple of seats away from where he used to sit in the chamber.

Widdecombe's funeral was held earlier this month at Buckfast Abbey in Devon, which she described as her "safe haven", attended by about 100 family, friends and former colleagues .

Reform UK's leader Nigel Farage did not attend the service, reportedly to avoid being a distraction, but he is said to be planning to visit a public memorial later this year.

Widdecombe's family are expected to release more details about the public memorial shortly.

Kerry is due to stand trial for murder in June 2027.

articles.title: New York mayor Mamdani makes a stink over RSS event, stirs up row among Indian diaspora
articles.summary: US News: WASHINGTON/NEW DELHI: New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani has stirred up a row among sections of the diaspora – and between Indian political parties – .
articles.body: WASHINGTON/NEW DELHI: New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani has stirred up a row among sections of the diaspora – and between Indian political parties – by declaring that he does not support a planned Aug 29 appearance by RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat at MSG, while conceding that his office probably cannot cancel it.The gathering, billed as the 'Universal Oneness Celebration' and organised by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue, is expected to draw about 5,000 Indian Americans during the RSS’s centenary-year global outreach. “I don’t support the rally, but I don’t know if the city has any jurisdiction on cancelling a private event,” Mamdani told reporters Tuesday, amid left-liberal opposition to the event and demands to cancel it.Mamdani, New York’s first Indian-American and Muslim mayor (and son of film-maker Mira Nair and Ugandan-Indian Mahmood Mamdani), framed his opposition as a clash of competing visions. “The vision of India that I was taught by my family” was of “a pluralistic society, of a secular republic” in which everyone belonged, he said. The rise of a movement based on an “exclusionary vision,” he added, was “incredibly troubling.”In India, BJP MP Bhola Singh called Mamdani’s characterisation “incorrect and baseless”. “RSS has been continuously engaged in social service and nation-building for a very long time,” he said. BJP spokesperson Syed Zafar Islam termed the mayor’s statement “divisive”, while MP Yogender Chandolia said Bhagwat led a social organisation.Support crossed Maharashtra’s political divide. Shiv Sena (UBT) spokesperson Anand Dubey said opposition to an Indian leader abroad was “unwarranted”. Shiv Sena’s Shaina NC accused Mamdani of “appeasement politics” and cited work by RSS-linked service bodies in the US. Party leader Sanjay Nirupam went further, using the term “jihadi” for the mayor.However, TMC MP Saugata Roy said RSS ideology would not work in multi-religious New York. Congress MP Imran Masood questioned the purpose and global message of the event, while senior Congress politician from Maharashtra Nana Patole sought answers about the RSS’s structure, funding and Bhagwat’s visit.Bhagwat’s scheduled address is the centrepiece of the US leg of a three-country tour marking RSS’s centenary. The Sangh said the visit to the US, Canada and UK is intended to present what it called a factual view of India, Hindu society and RSS, counter “misinformation”, carry the message of “Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam” (the world as one family), and deepen engagement with the diaspora. Community leadership programmes are planned in Toronto and London.American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue said more than 200 Hindu-American organisations are supporting the 'Universal Oneness Celebration'. A coalition of 61 civil rights, religious and community groups has, however, asked Madison Square Garden to cancel it.Former Seattle City Council member Kshama Sawant, a prominent socialist, called Bhagwat one of India’s “most prominent and dangerous” far-right Hindu fundamentalist leaders and urged Mamdani to cancel the event. Pushback came from Mary Millben, an African-American singer who frequently performs India’s national anthem at events, as she accused Mamdani and “all these socialist nuts” of opposing the event because they oppose Modi and the BJP. Madison Square Garden “doesn’t answer to socialist rants,” she sneered, telling the mayor and his allies to “become capitalists, raise money” and rent the Garden themselves.The sparring reflects a long-running American divide over the RSS. Critics in the US accuse it of fostering an atmosphere hostile to minorities. The US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF), an independent bipartisan federal commission recently recommended that the US govt impose targeted sanctions on RSS. However, American diplomats and political figures have periodically engaged with RSS functionaries in India and during their visits to the US. Indeed, the Obama administration opposed a 2015 court effort to compel the State Department to designate it a foreign terrorist organisation. Most recently, senior RSS functionary Ram Madhav and general secretary Dattatreya Hosabale made US visits in April, meeting with think tanks, academics, and policy experts.Pro-RSS groups maintain that the organisation is a cultural and voluntary movement and point to its extensive charitable and disaster-relief work in America. Some also accuse the American progressive left of a double standard: being extraordinarily vigilant about so-called Hindu nationalism while being more permissive toward radical Islamist or pro-Hamas activism. For now, however, the Bhagwat rally is likely to proceed – not because Mamdani approves of it, but because in America, disapproval is not a cancellation notice.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Watch: Buckingham Palace pays tribute to music legend Dolly Parton with surprise ‘9 to 5’ performance
articles.summary: UK News: Buckingham Palace paid tribute to music icon Dolly Parton on August 26, 2026, with a surprise performance of her song '9 to 5' during the Changing of the Guard ceremony, celebrating her vast charitable contributions and her love for reading.
articles.body: Buckingham Palace paid tribute to American singer Dolly Parton on Wednesday as the Band of the Coldstream Guards performed her iconic song “9 To 5” during the Changing of the Guard ceremony.The Royal Family later shared footage of the performance on its official social media accounts, remembering Parton for her music as well as her charitable work.“Remembering the late, great Dolly, who brought joy, comfort and inspiration to so many including the millions of children given free books through her Imagination Library. We will always love you,” the post said.Parton died on Tuesday. Her nephew Bryan Seaver confirmed her passing in a video shared on her official Instagram account. Parton was 80. Her representatives later said she had died following a brief battle with cancer.Parton's Imagination Library was also highlighted in tributes from the Royal Family. The programme has provided free books to children for decades, becoming one of the singer's most prominent philanthropic projects.The Queen's Reading Room, a charity founded by Queen Camilla, also paid tribute to Parton, describing her as an advocate for reading and highlighting the scale of her work encouraging children to develop a love of books.“Today we remember and celebrate the unwavering advocate for the joy and importance of reading – the icon, Dolly Parton,” the charity said.King Charles and Queen Camilla were not at Buckingham Palace during Wednesday's ceremony as they were spending their annual summer break at Balmoral. The Union Jack, rather than the Royal Standard, was flying above the Palace.During the ceremony, Number 12 Company Irish Guards marched from Wellington Barracks with the Band of the Coldstream Guards to take over duty from the outgoing guard.Parton's death has prompted tributes from across the music and entertainment world. She had continued working despite health problems and had spoken publicly about her determination to keep creating shortly before her death.Parton's husband, Carl Dean, died aged 82 in March 2025. articles.title: Meta-morphosis: FB puts kids on digital detox after coughing up $ 17.1 billion in settlement
articles.summary: US News: The TOI correspondent from Washington: For years, Facebook, Instagram, Tik-Tok, YouTube and other social media majors have laid out something like an .
articles.body: The TOI correspondent from Washington: For years, Facebook, Instagram, Tik-Tok, YouTube and other social media majors have laid out something like an all-you-can-eat binge buffet for teenagers: unlimited scrolling, notifications at all hours, and a boundless appetite for engagement.On Wednesday, Meta agreed to put some limits on the feast. The owner of Instagram and Facebook agreed to pay up to $17 billion to settle a landmark multistate lawsuit accusing it of deliberately designing its platforms to hook children, concealing the risks and improperly collecting data from youngsters.In return, Meta will impose some of the most sweeping restrictions yet on how American teenagers use its platforms. The settlement requires a default two-hour daily limit for users under 18, with parents able to override it. Instagram and Facebook will also get a digital bedtime: access will be restricted between midnight and 6 am, while notifications will be curtailed at night and during school hours. Likes and reaction counts on posts by minors will disappear, cosmetic-surgery filters will be banned for young users, age-assurance systems and parental controls will be strengthened, and Meta will interrupt the infinite-scroll experience. In other words, the company that spent years perfecting the art of making teenagers say “just five more minutes” will now have to help enforce bedtime.Teenagers will also be offered the option of a non-personalized feed, rather than one driven by algorithms designed to predict -- and presumably prolong -- their engagement. An independent auditor will monitor compliance. Meta has also agreed to stop making misleading claims about the safety of its platforms.Meta is initially expected to pay roughly $12.7 billion, with the total potentially reaching $17.1 billion depending on whether rival platforms such as TikTok and YouTube adopt comparable measures and contribute financially. While it is an enormous number ($17.1 billion is about Rs 1.6 lakh crores), it is also chump change by Meta standards. Taking into account the company reported about $201 billion in revenue in 2025, the settlement looks less like a corporate extinction event than a reminder that even Silicon Valley has lawyers' bills.The case began in 2023 when attorneys general from 29 states sued Meta in federal court, alleging that Facebook and Instagram had been deliberately engineered to keep children and teenagers compulsively hooked. The states accused the company of knowing that its products could contribute to mental and physical harm while misleading parents and the public about those dangers. They also alleged violations of federal child-privacy law through the collection of information from children under 13 without appropriate parental consent.The original coalition was bipartisan and grew into a much larger settlement involving 47 states, the US Capital and several U.S. territories. The trial, which began only last week, was supposed to continue for weeks, potentially putting CEO Mark Zuckerberg on the witness stand, before Wednesday's legal equivalent of the emergency exit.The case had become particularly uncomfortable for Meta after testimony from Arturo Bejar, a former safety engineer. who told the court that he repeatedly raised concerns about harmful experiences affecting young users and alleged that Meta's culture prioritized engagement and growth over safety. He portrayed a company that understood the problem but struggled to put child welfare ahead of the machinery that generated advertising revenue. The allegations were hardly isolated. Previous revelations had already exposed internal concerns about Instagram's effects on teenagers, particularly girls and issues involving body image and mental health.Critics are now alleging that social media companies have effectively created digital opioids for children: products engineered to exploit the same basic human vulnerabilities that make gambling, cigarettes and addictive drugs so profitable. The accusation is not simply that teenagers happen to spend too much time online; it is that the business model rewards companies for discovering what keeps a child clicking, scrolling, comparing, reacting and returning.Seen that way, Meta was not merely a negligent babysitter; it was, in the words of one critic, like a rogue pharma outlet, deliberately providing digital opioids to youth while insisting that everyone was enjoying themselves. Others likened the settlement pushing the toothpaste back into the tube.Still, the settlement may prove to be an important turning point. For the first time, a major social-media company has been forced to alter fundamental features of its products as part of a nationwide legal settlement over harm to youth. Meta's agreement could also increase pressure on TikTok, YouTube, and others who face scores of lawsuits of their own from states, school districts and individuals. The first pebble has rolled down the mountain -- the question now is whether Wednesday's settlement is the end or the precursor to an avalanche.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Dolly Parton's gift of reading to 1,000 Manx kids
articles.summary: More than 1,000 Manx children still receive free books through Dolly Parton's Imagination Library
articles.body:
More than 1,000 children on the Isle of Man have recieved books through Dolly Parton's Imagination Library since the scheme launched in Douglas at Christmas.

It posts a free book to every registered child each month until they turn five, and has since spread across most of the island's parishes.

Parton - a country star whose literacy campaigns have brought books to millions of children around the globe - died this week, aged 80.

"Dolly's vision has already had an extraordinary impact here on the Isle of Man," said Trish McDonough, who has been coordinating the scheme's roll-out locally.

Parton launched the Imagination Library in 1995 in her home county in Tennessee, as a tribute to her father, Robert Lee Parton, a sharecropper who never learned to read or write.

She called him "the smartest man I have ever known," but felt his illiteracy had held him back from his own ambitions.

Parton had hoped the scheme might, in her words, "go a couple of counties over," but it grew into a global programme reaching more than three million children a month.

"We feel incredibly privileged to play a part in continuing her legacy here on the Isle of Man," McDonough said.

Every baby born at the Jane Crookall Maternity Unit has automatically received a book since the end of February.

Registrations first opened in Douglas at Christmas, with the first books arriving in February.

More than 1,00 children have registered since launch, with 972 currently receiving books, and 54 who have since turned five and "graduated" from the scheme.

More than 3,500 books have been delivered to children across the island, with a further 871 on order for September.

Andreas, Ballaugh, Bride, Jurby, Lezayre and Maughold joined the scheme in March, after a community crowdfunding campaign was started locally.

Patrick, Marown, Port Erin, Port St Mary, Arbory and Rushen, Santon, Michael and Peel have all joined since.

Ramsey is now the subject of an active crowdfunding campaign, with organisers hoping to bring the Imagination Library to the town next.

articles.title: Iran emphasises self-sufficiency in battle against US economic war
articles.summary: Iranian authorities believe they can withstand US sanctions, but warn of a tough year ahead.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – Iranian authorities are adamant that their country’s domestic capacities will be able to keep the country’s economy afloat, despite new economic sanctions targeting Iran unveiled by the United States this week.

The US aims to use the sanctions to force Iran into submission in the six month-long war between the two countries. But Iran’s government says it is prepared, with Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh referring to a two-year plan on state television on Monday night.

“We have our own tools and we also know the game,” Madanizadeh said, in reference to Iran’s years of experience in trying to circumvent sanctions. He added that Tehran could potentially “go on the offensive” in a world where the US was no longer the only dominant force, and was confidant that many countries would effectively reject US President Donald Trump’s threats to cut off all links with Iran .

Stockpiling essential goods, foreign currencies and gold has become a main tactic for Tehran. The government has also been forced to resort to rationing energy in one of the most resource-rich countries in the world.

Central Bank Governor Abdolnasser Hemmati told senior business representatives during a meeting earlier this week that oil exports, Iran’s main foreign currency income source, have almost totally stopped. But Hemmati reassured the business leaders there was no shortage of foreign currency for essential goods as the central bank had cash stockpiles “in places [the US] cannot access”.

Hemmati acknowledged “serious issues” like runaway inflation and constantly declining purchasing power for the people, but said, “enduring hardship is very different from collapse and what the US is after”.

Iranians must not expect conditions to get any better over the next year, government spokesman Fatemeh Mohajerani told state-linked media on Tuesday. She also said Iran’s Supreme National Security Council would have to grant authorisation for the government to reveal data on poverty levels in the country.

Iran’s national currency fell to a new all-time low of 2.05 million rials against the US dollar on the open market on Tuesday, before slightly recovering on Wednesday.

Despite the turmoil, Iran’s newly-appointed security chief Mohsen Rezaei urged younger Iranians during a state TV interview earlier this week to “enter the economy” and begin manufacturing goods needed by their households and communities at home.

That mentality has permeated the Islamic Republic’s strategic thinking for decades, with national development plans repeatedly emphasising “self-sufficiency” and setting targets to achieve it at great cost.

To reduce its reliance on food imports for a population of around 90 million, the government claims that Iran can produce 85 percent of its agricultural products domestically, even as concerns remain over what the increase in domestic agricultural production means for Iran’s dire water scarcity problems .

Agriculture Minister Gholam-Reza Nouri said on state television on Tuesday that Tehran aimed to increase domestic food self-sufficiency to 90 percent in the short-term, ahead of ultimately producing all of the country’s essential food domestically.

Nouri said that Iran imports about $16bn and exports $8bn in agricultural products – although exports of some products were suspended in March shortly after the start of the war.

Iran relies on imports for essential foods and feed commodities, including wheat, maize, rice and vegetable oils. The United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia are among Iran’s top suppliers of refined sugar and wheat flour through re-export hubs. Russia and Central Asia can also provide some grain through the Caspian Sea into northern Iran.

The United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization said in March that rising import costs, logistics disruptions and policy responses aimed at protecting domestic supply are accelerating food inflation and reducing household purchasing power in Iran. It also warned that overland trade routes do not have the capacity to replace the much larger volumes of goods normally transported by sea.

Food prices in Iran were more than 128 percent higher in July than they were a year earlier, according to the latest report by the Statistical Center of Iran. The same amount of money now buys far less food in Tehran and across the country than it did six months ago.

Iran’s government also says the country produces some 97 percent of its medicine, although imported medicines account for a much larger share of total pharmaceutical spending.

Salman Eshaghi, spokesman of the parliament’s health committee, said in May that Iran faced some levels of shortages for nearly 1,000 medicines. Medicine prices have also surged over recent months, including this week, after the government confirmed that it was gradually cutting off cheap currency allocation to some imports .

Iran’s authorities have said they are working quickly to repair some of the damage dealt to Iran’s infrastructure during the war, including to oil, gas and utility facilities extensively bombed by the US and Israel.

The was has compounded Iran’s existing energy shortages and infrastructure problems.

Daily power blackouts continue to plague households and industrial units in Tehran and cities across the country, while natural gas shortages are expected to hit within a few months when the weather gets colder and demand rises.

On Tuesday and Wednesday, a considerable number of petrol stations in Tehran, Mashhad, Karaj and several other cities also ran out of fuel allocated to them by the government, leading to lengthy queues.

Government spokesperson Mohajerani on Wednesday promised that existing fuel prices and quota levels would remain unchanged through the end of the current Iranian calendar month on September 22. But the government has already cut fuel quotas for private vehicles.

The National Iranian Oil Refining and Distribution Company promised on Wednesday that the inauguration of two new refineries in southern Iran by the end of the current year in late March would add about 12 million litres per day to Iran’s production capacity, helping offset some of the shortage.

Iran’s government has no choice but to engage in “painful reforms” by increasing fuel prices in order to avoid another “bloodshed” during social unrest, Iranian economist Sadegh Alhosseini warned in a speech on Tuesday.

“If Iran heads toward large-scale chaos – kilometres-long petrol queues and becoming like Venezuela – something much worse will happen that will be much more difficult to handle,” he said.

But another fuel cost hike will further increase inflation by ramping up transport costs, and many people are already struggling to get by. Iran may continue to withstand historic levels of pressure, but it is becoming increasingly vulnerable to a cycle in which its resources and capacity are steadily depleted.

articles.title: Bangladesh: Hindu businessman, 4 family members go missing amid threats
articles.summary: South Asia News: A Hindu businessman and four members of his family have been missing from Bangladesh's Chandpur district since August 20, with police investigating re.
articles.body: A Hindu businessman and four members of his family have been missing from Bangladesh's Chandpur district since August 20, with police investigating reports that he had received threats, according to local media reports.Pintu Das, who runs a shop and is also involved in lending money against gold jewellery, went missing along with his wife, two teenage sons and another family member, bdnews.com reported, citing police."I have learned that Pintu Das and four members of his family have been missing since August 20," Chandpur Model Police Station officer-in-charge Foyez Ahmed said, according to news agency PTI.Ahmed said there were allegations that several people had not received their gold back after pledging jewellery with Das. However, he said the circumstances surrounding the family's disappearance were still being investigated."We will only be able to confirm after the investigation if Pintu Das and his family members have gone into hiding voluntarily or if something else has happened to them," Ahmed said.Upama Dey, Chandpur chapter leader of the Hindu Buddhist Christian Unity Council (HBCUC) and Das' cousin, said he disappeared from his rented house in Chandpur along with his wife and two sons, who are Class 10 students."We have heard that he received threats as he was under a burden with debt," she said, adding that Das' ancestral home is in southeastern Chattogram.The disappearance comes amid renewed concerns over the safety of Bangladesh's Hindu minority following the killing of a Hindu family in Rangpur last week.Four-member Hindu family killed in RangpurA retired Hindu schoolteacher, his wife and their two children were found dead inside their locked home in Rangpur last week. The victims were identified as 65-year-old Ganapati Chakraborty, his wife Pritilata, 50, their daughter Agami Chakraborty Prarthi, 23, and their 12-year-old son Priyam Chakraborty.Police arrested two suspects, identified as Mugdha and Siddhartha, in connection with the killings. Investigators said the suspects allegedly entered the house to take yaba and killed the family after Ganapati confronted them.Police said the suspects remained inside the house after the killings and later scattered furniture, clothes and other belongings to make the incident appear like a robbery.The suspects allegedly left the house on Friday during Jummah prayers, when the streets were relatively empty, local media reported.Police said gold jewellery allegedly taken from the house was later recovered from a location identified by the suspects. Date pits found at the scene were also sent for DNA testing.The bodies were recovered from different parts of the house. Police said the mother and daughter were found on the staircase, Ganapati's body was found on the roof and Priyam's body was recovered from under a bed.Subir Chowdhury, in-charge of Rangpur Metropolitan CID, said, "The household belongings were found scattered and in disarray. For now, it appears to be a robbery. However, nothing can be confirmed until the investigation is completed."The police account has, however, faced questions from minority rights activists, relatives and local residents. The investigation was subsequently transferred to the specialised detective branch."We are watching the developments. But it remains a big question how two alleged drug addicts could kill four people and give the house a look of a robbery scene in such a meticulous manner?," a leader of the Hindu Buddhist Christian Unity Council said.The latest incidents have renewed concerns over attacks on religious minorities in Bangladesh.According to a report by the US-based Human Rights Congress for Bangladesh Minorities (HRCBM), there were 824 verified incidents of human rights abuses, including 116 targeted killings, across 63 of Bangladesh's 64 districts during the first half of 2026.The report also cited attacks on 142 temples, looting of 209 homes and businesses, and 73 cases of forced land grabbing involving religious minorities.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Funeral held for renowned Palestinian artist Sliman Mansour
articles.summary: The 79-year-old was best known for paintings depicting the Palestinian landscape and cultural scenes featuring Palestinian symbols of identity.
articles.body:
The funeral has taken place at a packed church in Birzeit, near Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, for the celebrated Palestinian artist Sliman Mansour, who died this week at the age of 79.

He was best known for his bright and powerful paintings depicting the Palestinian landscape, with its olive groves and citrus trees, as well as cultural scenes featuring symbols of identity amid the nationalist struggle - the Palestinians' pursuit of self-determination, independence and statehood.

One of his most famous works is Camel of Hardship, painted in 1973. It shows an elderly porter carrying the burden of Jerusalem and the golden Dome of the Rock on his back.

"He was actually the main Palestinian artist, the best known locally and internationally," recalled his friend and fellow artist Vera Tamari.

Tamari said Mansour's work showed "Palestine in all its beauty and hope".

"He portrayed the Palestinian woman in her thobe - her traditional embroidered costume - and he portrayed people very much attached to the land," she went on. "He wanted people to know that we are rooted here."

Mansour was born in the village of Birzeit in British Mandate Palestine in 1947 – a year before the State of Israel was established, and the advent of the first Arab-Israeli war. During the conflict, more than 700,000 Palestinians were expelled from their homes or fled in what is known as the Nakba, "the Catastrophe".

As a young man, Mansour studied fine art in Jerusalem but went on to develop his own distinctive style. He has spoken of how Palestinian artists lived in a "cultural ghetto" and how he was influenced by a book showing works of the Mexican painter Diego Rivera.

Over time, Mansour contributed to creating a local artistic movement, as co-founder of the League of Palestinian Artists and the International Academy of Art and helping to set up local art galleries.

As well as his paintings on canvas, Mansour created cartoons, children's illustrations and wrote books. Many remember him as an inspiring art teacher.

His works are held in private collections and at major international institutions including the Guggenheim Museum in Abu Dhabi, the Mathaf: Arab Museum of Modern Art in Doha, the Institut du Monde Arabe in Paris, and the British Museum in London.

However, unlike many artists, Mansour was also strongly in favour of his paintings being reproduced as prints, making them more accessible and adding to their wide appreciation.

"He was the mastermind of creating a Palestine that unifies us all as Palestinians, something that we long for and we work to live in," said Amer Shomali, a visual artist and director general of the Palestinian Museum.

"I grew up in a refugee camp in Syria," he continued. "As a child, I had two of his posters on my wall. He was everywhere. He was focusing and capitalising on reaching the masses.

"He liked the idea that [his work] was being displayed by people who could afford it all around the world."

The political nature of Palestinian art often drew the attention of Israeli security forces in the occupied West Bank. In a podcast, Mansour spoke about how in the 1970s and 1980s soldiers would confiscate posters and postcards, arresting the sellers.

When a new space for solo exhibitions, Gallery 79, was founded in Ramallah, he said: "The soldiers started coming to the opening of every new exhibition and sometimes taking whatever they didn't like."

"We developed a kind of art that is symbolic so that people will understand what we mean and the soldiers will not understand," he commented.

During the first intifada or uprising, which began in 1987, Mansour helped found the New Vision collective with other artists, including Tamari. Boycotting Israeli-made supplies including oil and acrylic paints, they turned increasingly to natural materials from clay to henna.

"Sliman specialised in working in mud and straw in very effective cracked surfaces, which reminded people of history and time and the rootedness of Palestine in the earth itself," Tamari said.

Friends remember a soft-spoken, humble man with a gift for explaining complex ideas in a simple way and who loved to share his work.

Although his canvases typically sell for hundreds of thousands of dollars, when he completed a large mural for the Palestinian Museum, his requested fee was only a fig tree to be planted in the garden.
